title: The true meaning of common idioms: satirical decoder for business-speak and empty marketing copy
summary: A humorous glossary translating common business idioms into what people actually mean. Mostly comedy, but it skewers jargon-stuffed positioning and "leading provider" boilerplate, and shows how polite non-answers ("Yes, but...", "Duly noted") usually mean "no."

principles.text: Jargon-stuffed company descriptions signal that you don't know what you do; say it plainly instead.
principles.quote: I have no idea what we do. Please give me money.

principles.text: "Leading provider" is filler that says nothing; it's what you write when you have no real differentiator to state.
principles.quote: I can't think of anything else to say, and the lawyers tell me I can't say "the" leading provider.

principles.text: Hedged prospect replies like "Yes, but..." or "Maybe, and..." almost always mean no; don't mistake politeness for interest.
"Duly noted" means the other side has already decided no; further persuasion is wasted effort.
principles.quote: Stop trying to convince me; I've already decided "no."

principles.text: Hope is not a strategy; "it is what it is" signals a team with no plan to fix a mistake.
principles.quote: We screwed up and have no idea how to fix it.
